decision_context: On 27 January 1986, immediately before Morton Thiokol communicates its final oral recommendation at approximately 11 p.m. Eastern Standard Time, contractor management and NASA are deciding whether STS-51L should launch the next morning under temperatures well below previous shuttle flight experience. Thiokol engineering has initially recommended no launch below 53°F because of concern about solid-rocket-booster field-joint O-ring sealing.
decision_question: Should Morton Thiokol maintain its engineering no-launch recommendation, recommend launch, or require delay/further review?
available_actions: Maintain the recommendation not to launch until O-ring conditions are within demonstrated flight experience.
Reverse the recommendation and approve the next-morning launch despite colder conditions.
Delay launch to a later time/date with warmer conditions if other mission constraints allow.
Defer recommendation pending additional analysis and escalation of unresolved engineering dissent to higher launch-management levels.

affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Life and safety in an irreversible crewed launch.
Professional duty to communicate technical risk and have safety objections represented accurately.
Mission schedule, programme commitments, organisational reputation, cost and safety responsibility.
Mission benefits, public resources, trust and consequences of catastrophic failure.

known_evidence.claim: Forecast launch conditions are substantially colder than prior shuttle flight experience; local ambient temperature was forecast in the mid-20s °F near launch time.
known_evidence.confidence_note: Weather forecasts available during the teleconference.

known_evidence.claim: Thiokol engineering reports that lower temperature slows the O-ring sealing response and initially recommends no launch below 53°F, the coldest prior relevant flight experience.
The coldest prior flight had shown the worst observed primary O-ring blow-by, supporting concern about cold performance.
NASA challenges a simple temperature correlation: another flight at a warmer temperature had also shown blow-by, and a colder static motor test showed no observed blow-by/erosion.
known_evidence.confidence_note: The relevance of the static test is disputed because its preparation differed from flight conditions.

known_evidence.claim: Participants describe the temperature data as inconclusive and disagree about whether those data justify launch in the forecast conditions.
NASA managers raise operational consequences of accepting a 53°F constraint, including effects on launch frequency and future operations.

Allan McDonald argues that lower temperatures worsen O-ring sealing performance. At Kennedy Space Center, while Thiokol managers deliberate separately, he proposes delaying to warmer conditions; local NASA officials say that a later window has been considered and rejected because of abort-site weather or visibility constraints.

known_uncertainties: The exact relationship between temperature and probability/severity of joint-seal failure.
Whether static-test performance is sufficiently representative of the flight joint under forecast conditions.
Whether a precise safe minimum temperature can be established from the available data.
Whether delaying to warmer conditions is operationally feasible without creating other unacceptable mission risks.
Whether McDonald's local delay proposal has been communicated to Thiokol managers during their separate deliberation.
known_alternatives: Delay until temperature is within demonstrated flight experience.
Attempt a later launch window with warmer temperatures if abort-site/weather constraints permit.
Escalate unresolved engineering objection and uncertainty to higher-level launch decision-makers explicitly.
Require additional analysis rather than treating inconclusive evidence as sufficient for launch.
requested_output: Assess what evidential burden is appropriate for an irreversible crewed launch.
Distinguish evidence of safety from absence of conclusive evidence of failure.
Identify whether schedule/customer considerations are morally relevant to the safety threshold.
Assess the reversible alternatives and the treatment of engineering dissent.
Give a Moral Code decision without using later knowledge of the mission outcome.
